description: The collected poems that fixed the tramp poet's place in the Georgian lyric. It is a verse work of 1916 by W. H. Davies; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under georgian anthology lyric.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers the lyrics of the road, the hedge and the sky from the earlier collections, with the war lyrics of 1914-16, and fixed Davies's place among the Georgian poets as the plain voice of the open air.
narrative_structure: A collected edition of the lyrics, ordered by collection and by subject. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative.
literary_form: Poetry collection (collected)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain short line and the plain word.
historical_context: England in the war years, and the Georgian anthologies. The record dates the work as composed between 1905 and 1916 and first published in 1916 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric, it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric.
literary_significance: The 1916 Collected Poems fixed Davies's canon and his reputation: its lyrics of the roadside and the sky are the standard text of the tramp poet and the measure of the Georgian lyric from below.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Henry Davies. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.

title: Façade
description: The settings of the poems to Walton's music: the most performed experiment of English verse. It is a verse work of 1922 by Edith Sitwell; it belongs to Vorticism and the Modernist Little Magazine and it is catalogued here under modernist lyric and the new idiom; nonsense verse and the parody of rule and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Façade sets Edith Sitwell's poems - the horn, the polka, the waltz, the yodelling song - to be spoken through the Sengerphone to William Walton's instrumental music, so that the sound of the poem is the poem; the first performance of 1923 made it the most argued-over experiment of English verse.
narrative_structure: A suite of settings for speaking voice and instrumental music, in numbers. A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
principal_characters: Sir Beelzebub; Old Sir Faulk; Black Mrs Behemoth; Daisy and Lily ('Waltz'); Lily O'Grady ('Popular Song'); Mr Wagg ('Polka'); Jumbo ('Lullaby for Jumbo'); the Man from a Far Countree; the reciting voice behind the curtain
literary_form: Verse suite for speaking voice with Walton's music (first performed 1923)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is the poem as a pattern of sound: assonance, consonant-chime and the sprung line.
historical_context: London in 1922-23, and the modernist experiment of the spoken poem. The record dates the work as composed between 1920 and 1922 and first published in 1922 and first performed in 1923 and the corpus places it within Vorticism and the Modernist Little Magazine; Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: Façade is the most performed experiment in the history of English verse: its settings made the sound of the poem its subject and gave English modernism its most original collaboration, and the suite remains the test case of the poem as music.
